title: Probability Graph Modeling Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic graph modeling algorithm designed to automatically identify and model complex relationships and dependencies within data. The algorithm leverages the power of probability graphs to represent and analyze data, offering significant advantages over traditional methods in machine learning and recommendation systems. The core mechanism centers on constructing and refining probabilistic graphs to capture intricate connections and dependencies, ultimately enhancing the performance of these systems. This research aims to provide a robust and adaptable framework for data exploration and modeling, with the potential for widespread application across diverse fields.

title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks via Adversarial Training with Temporal Consistency Loss
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to enhancing the robustness of neural networks against adversarial attacks by incorporating a temporal consistency loss during adversarial training. Traditional adversarial training focuses primarily on minimizing the difference between the network's output for a clean input and its output after applying an adversarial perturbation. However, this approach often fails to address the issue of temporal vulnerability – the susceptibility of a network to adversarial attacks when presented with temporally shifted versions of the input. Our method addresses this limitation by adding a temporal consistency loss that explicitly penalizes changes in the network's output when the input is shifted in time. This results in a network that is not only resistant to immediate adversarial perturbations but also resilient to attacks that exploit temporal dependencies. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and illustrate its performance with a conceptual framework, highlighting the improved robustness compared to standard adversarial training. The core claim is that neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that can disrupt their performance. The core mechanism is training a neural network with an adversarial training strategy, incorporating a temporal consistency loss that penalizes changes in the network's output when presented with temporally shifted inputs, enhancing robustness to adversarial perturbations. This work represents a new combination of techniques for achieving greater network resilience.

title: Symbolic Regression with Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) is a powerful technique for discovering mathematical equations from data. However, a significant limitation of traditional SR is its inability to effectively quantify the uncertainty associated with the learned equations and their parameters. This paper proposes a novel approach to SR that integrates Bayesian inference, enabling the estimation of confidence intervals for both the discovered mathematical expressions and their associated parameters. We introduce a framework where SR is performed within a Bayesian framework, allowing us to model the prior distributions of the parameters and the likelihood of the data given the equation. The resulting posterior distribution provides a comprehensive quantification of uncertainty. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and illustrate its capabilities with a simplified example. The core claim is that integrating Bayesian inference into SR significantly improves its ability to provide reliable and informative results by explicitly addressing the uncertainty inherent in the process. This work represents a crucial step towards more robust and trustworthy SR systems.

title: Composable Neural Program Synthesis with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Neural program synthesis, the automated generation of neural networks from high-level specifications, holds immense potential for simplifying deep learning development and enabling new forms of AI. However, the complexity of neural network architectures and the vastness of the possible compositions pose a significant challenge. This work presents a novel approach to neural program synthesis leveraging reinforcement learning (RL). Our system employs an RL agent to learn the art of composing neural networks by selecting and connecting primitive operations (e.g., convolution, pooling, ReLU) from a predefined library. The agent's actions are guided by a reward function that directly optimizes the accuracy of the synthesized program on a given task. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach, showcasing its ability to generate reasonably accurate neural networks for various tasks. The core innovation lies in the integration of RL for guided exploration of the compositional space, offering a practical solution to the inherent difficulties of neural program synthesis. We define the problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and formalize the agent's learning process using RL algorithms. The system's performance is evaluated on a range of benchmark datasets, highlighting its potential for automated neural network design.

title: Probability Geometry Algorithms: An Adaptive Optimization Approach
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic geometry algorithm leveraging the power of deep learning to automatically optimize geometric parameters crucial for complex physical models. We propose an adaptive optimization framework, integrating probabilistic geometry with neural networks, enabling the algorithm to dynamically adjust parameters to enhance the strength and stability of specific geometric structures. The core mechanism centers around training a deep neural network to learn the optimal parameters for each geometric configuration, facilitating automated parameter tuning and improved results. This approach offers a significant advancement over existing methods, particularly in scenarios requiring intricate geometric modeling and complex physics simulations. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this algorithm through illustrative examples and analysis, highlighting its potential to streamline the design and analysis of numerous physical systems.

title: Formal Semantic Network Reasoning Engine
abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of a formal semantic network reasoning engine. The core of the engine is built upon the principles of formal logic and automated reasoning, specifically utilizing Description Logics and ontology reasoning techniques. The system's primary function is to automatically construct knowledge chains from semantic networks and subsequently address complex data querying challenges. The key innovation lies in elevating semantic network inference to a logical level, resulting in more precise and reliable knowledge extraction and reasoning capabilities. This approach moves beyond traditional rule-based systems, offering a more robust and scalable solution for knowledge representation and inference. The engine utilizes a formalized knowledge graph derived from the semantic network, facilitating the application of automated reasoning mechanisms to derive new insights and answer intricate queries. The paper details the architecture, logical framework, and core mechanisms of the engine, demonstrating its potential for applications requiring sophisticated knowledge integration and reasoning.

title: Based on Differential Geometry: A Neural Network Architecture Design
abstract: This paper proposes a novel neural network architecture design rooted in the principles of differential geometry. The core idea is to treat the network's layered structure as a geometric space and leverage concepts such as curvature and tensors to guide the optimization process. Traditional neural network architecture design often relies heavily on empirical rules and heuristics, lacking the rigorous theoretical foundation provided by differential geometry. This approach aims to improve the network's ability to capture inherent geometric structures within data, potentially leading to enhanced performance in various tasks. We introduce a framework for constructing these geometric neural networks, outlining the key components and their mathematical formulation. The proposed architecture seeks to move beyond purely data-driven design, offering a more principled and potentially more effective method for neural network construction. ---

title: Information-Theoretic Graph Embedding for Anomaly Detection
abstract: Anomaly detection in complex networks, such as social networks, financial networks, and biological networks, is a critical task with widespread applications. Traditional anomaly detection methods often rely on statistical measures or graph-based approaches that may not fully capture the intricate information flow and dependencies within the network. This paper proposes a novel approach to anomaly detection based on information-theoretic graph embedding. We leverage information-theoretic metrics like mutual information (MI), transfer entropy (TE), and adjacency spectral embedding to learn graph embeddings that explicitly represent the underlying information structure of the network. These embeddings are then used to identify anomalies, which manifest as deviations from the expected information flow patterns. The core idea is that anomalies disrupt the normal information exchanges, and by embedding the network using information-theoretic measures, we can directly quantify and detect these disruptions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through theoretical analysis and provide a framework for further research in this area. The methodology presented offers a more robust and principled approach than existing methods, particularly in scenarios where the underlying structure of the network is complex and poorly understood. The key contributions are the integration of information theory into graph embedding and the development of a novel anomaly detection framework based on these embeddings.

title: Title: Self-Healing Modular Systems for Computational Models
abstract: The creation and maintenance of computational models is a complex and time-consuming process, often requiring significant manual intervention. This paper proposes a novel system, termed "Self-Healing Modular Systems," designed to automate this process, focusing on the creation and updating of models with built-in self-correction mechanisms. The core concept revolves around the implementation of a system of "mutation agents" that iteratively refine the model based on observed errors, guided by genetic algorithms. This approach aims to drastically improve the reliability of simulations by mitigating model degradation and facilitating continuous improvement. The system's effectiveness will be demonstrated through a focused investigation of model fidelity and stability.

title: 基于拓扑场的量子计算验证协议
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum computation verification protocol based on topological quantum structure. Traditional verification methods rely on static parameters, while this protocol leverages the dynamic adjustment of quantum computation's correctness to enhance its security. We present a framework demonstrating the potential for improved verification through the inherent robustness of topological quantum systems. The core mechanism involves constructing and analyzing topological quantum states to establish and validate the correctness of quantum algorithms. This approach offers a more adaptable and secure verification strategy compared to conventional methods. The research explores the practical implications of this protocol and highlights its potential impact on the robustness of quantum computation.

title: Neuromodulated state space models: a dopamine-inspired selective gating framework with memory–stability trade-offs
abstract: Dopamine shapes how the prefrontal cortex filters incoming information, maintains it in working memory, and releases it for action — three computational roles that closely parallel the input, state, and output stages of a sequence model. Here we ask whether formalizing this correspondence yields a sequence architecture that is both computationally competitive and mechanistically interpretable in biological terms. We introduce the Neuromodulated State Space Model (NeuSSM), which reinterprets the selective gating mechanism of modern state space models (e.g., Mamba) as three dopamine-inspired operators — sensory gating, working-memory modulation, and output relay — controlled by a single learnable gain parameter λ. We show theoretically that the classical S4 model arises as a limiting case of NeuSSM at λ = 0 (Theorem 1), and that NeuSSM’s local dynamical stability is governed by a phase-transition criterion based on the real part of the modulated state-transition eigenvalues, which partitions the model’s worst-case behavior into three qualitatively distinct regimes (Theorem 2). Mamba-style selective architectures are recovered qualitatively as λ → 1, though we present this correspondence empirically rather than as a formal approximation guarantee. Training NeuSSM on four long-range sequence benchmarks (≈ 0.45 M parameters, single consumer GPU), we find that the model learns different λ values in different layers depending on the task, with tasks requiring more flexible, long-range reasoning driving higher λ in upper layers — a pattern consistent with the proposed dynamical-stability trade-off (Theorem 2). NeuSSM reaches 98.75% on Sequential MNIST, 49.45% on LRA ListOps, 59.88% on Sequential CIFAR-10, and 76.0% on LRA Text, competitive with or approaching much larger S4 and Mamba baselines at a fraction of the parameter count. These results suggest that neuromodulatory principles from systems neuroscience can inform both the design and the interpretation of sequence models, even at modest computational scale.

title: A Data Fusion Framework for Grounding Aerospace Surrogate Model via Experimental Wind-Tunnel Observations
abstract: Aerodynamic surrogate models trained on high-fidelity CFD data reproduce numerical predictions of both scalar outputs and entire fields accurately, yet their predictive fidelity is limited by systematic discrepancies between CFD and experimental observations. We present an experimentally grounded correction framework that adapts a CFD-trained deep learning surrogate using wind-tunnel PSP measurements. A Geotransolver surrogate trained on 2,300 high-fidelity CFD simulations of the NASA CRM wing-body configuration, spanning geometric variation, Mach 0.70-0.85, and angles of attack 0 to 4 degrees, reproduces the CFD integrated aerodynamic forces and pitching moment to R2 > 0.99 but does not match the experimental data. To incorporate experimental information without retraining the surrogate, a correction network is trained on spatially registered PSP measurements at two freestream Mach numbers (0.70 and 0.85) across the same angle-of-attack range, learning the discrepancy between the surrogate-predicted and experimentally measured surface-pressure distributions. At Mach 0.85 the correction substantially improves agreement with PSP, particularly at the wing suction peak, shock location, and subsequent pressure recovery, reducing both the magnitude of the prediction error and the fraction of wetted surface on which it exceeds 0.05 in Cp, and it does so from a limited experimental dataset without modifying the pretrained surrogate parameters. On held-out angles of attack the grounded surrogate agrees with measurement to within 2.3-2.7% of the measured Cp range, and outperforms direct interpolation between the measured conditions at every state tested. Experimental measurements can therefore ground a large-scale simulation-trained surrogate by learning systematic CFD-to-experiment discrepancies while preserving its generalization capability and computational efficiency.

title: Loom: Weaving Diagnostic Strands into Free-Text Consensus via Embedding-Space Reweighting
abstract: Aggregating noisy, conflicting textual hypotheses into a reliable consensus is a fundamental challenge when deploying NLP systems in real-world industrial settings. While monolithic Large Language Model (LLM) agents offer unbounded expressivity for tasks like Root Cause Analysis (RCA), they suffer from context limits, compounding hallucinations, and prohibitive inference latency. Traditional weak supervision offers statistical rigor but is mathematically restricted to discrete classes. We present Loom, a generative consensus framework deployed for real-world RCA that bridges these paradigms. Loom aggregates open-form hypotheses emitted by modular heuristics (diagnostic templates dynamically populated with episode-specific entities, times, and metrics) by projecting them into a continuous embedding space, and resolves conflicting signals with an iterative centroid-based reweighting algorithm. The resulting consensus weights ground a single lightweight LLM synthesis step. Evaluated on the OpenRCA benchmark, Loom occupies the accuracy--efficiency Pareto frontier: it matches a state-of-the-art autonomous agent on Bank and Market-2 and trails on Market-1 and Telecom, while using a single LLM call per incident on all four datasets ($\sim$26$\times$ faster; $\sim$33$\times$ with an 8B-parameter synthesizer). We discuss our deployment experience, highlighting lessons learned regarding the trade-offs between agentic depth and inference latency, negative results in redundancy detection, and how deterministic consensus fosters trust among Subject Matter Experts~(SMEs).

title: Programming anharmonic potentials in a superconducting harmonic oscillator
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum systems offer a resource-efficient route to universal quantum information processing and analogue quantum simulation of real-world processes, such as molecular physics and chemical reactions. Realising these applications, however, requires non-Gaussian operations that implement anharmonic potentials, which are challenging to engineer on demand. Here, we demonstrate a systematic framework to implement programmable non-Gaussian phase gates $e^{-iV(\hat{X})}$, corresponding to the impulsive action of a potential $V(\hat{X})$, in a superconducting harmonic oscillator coupled to a transmon qubit. Using modular circuits derived from bosonic quantum signal processing, we realise a range of target anharmonic potentials on a single piece of hardware by varying a set of qubit rotations interleaved with a fixed calibrated control unitary. We first demonstrate a cubic phase gate, a key ingredient for universal quantum information processing. The resulting high-fidelity non-Gaussian states and the potential reconstructed using our pointwise force reconstruction method jointly confirm the cubic nature of the target gate. We then engineer a family of double-well potentials, relevant models of tunnelling and biased transfer processes, and experimentally validate the double-well topology and the tunable asymmetry. Finally, we engineer an approximate Morse gate, a step towards realistic potentials of molecular vibrational systems, and provide a concrete path towards high-quality engineering and reconstruction of the exponential form. Together, these results establish a practical and reconfigurable route towards continuous-variable quantum information processing and anharmonic quantum simulation.

Finally, we engineer an approximate Morse gate, a step towards realistic potentials of molecular vibrational systems, and provide a concrete path towards high-quality engineering and reconstruction of the exponential form. Together, these results establish a practical and reconfigurable route towards continuous-variable quantum information processing and anharmonic quantum simulation.

title: TempoGround: State-Aware Streaming Visual Grounding with Vision-Language Models
abstract: Visual grounding maps language referents to spatial targets and is central to open-vocabulary perception with vision-language models. Existing methods have made substantial progress on single-frame and video-based visual grounding, yet under streaming inputs they still suffer from identity drift, cross-frame inconsistency, and fragile localization under partial occlusion. To address these issues, we present TempoGround, a VLM-native framework that detects cross-frame object correspondence and explicitly models object presence states, thereby enabling accurate and consistent visual grounding under streaming inputs. The key is a curriculum prediction mechanism guided by state-aware cross-frame correspondence: TempoGround resolves 2D instance association, predicts whether each object newly enters, continues in, or leaves the view, decodes the 2D box, and then lifts it to a camera-frame 3D box. As token-level supervision alone cannot capture the geometric objectives of streaming grounding, we further introduce Streaming Grounding Reinforcement (SGR), which optimizes TempoGround with verifiable Grounding, Identity, and Consistency rewards, jointly reinforcing persistent localization and temporally consistent predictions. We carefully design a three-stage training strategy and train TempoGround on large-scale data. We evaluate visual grounding under causally streaming inputs on multiple challenging benchmarks: TempoGround improves F1_2D@0.5 and F1_2D@0.95 by 4.4 and 0.5 on average, and F1_3D@0.25 and AP_3D by 6.2 and 7.5, respectively. These results demonstrate that TempoGround provides a practical foundation for visual grounding under streaming inputs.

title: Low-overhead tailoring and learning of noise in graph states
abstract: Graph and hypergraph states are important resource states for realizing universal quantum computation and diverse non-local physical phenomena. However, noise learning in such states is challenging due to their large entanglement and magic. This work establishes a low Clifford hierarchy circuit-based scheme for tailoring and learning noise in (hyper)graph states generated by multiple controlled-Z gates. The key is to convert the noisy input state into diagonal form and derive the convolution equation for the diagonal noise rates, which has a lower resource overhead. Such a diagonal form can be used in real quantum simulation by using the same conversion technique on the graph state input. We demonstrate that a single-depth Bell measurement is sufficient in our scheme for arbitrary graph states, while noise tailoring can be done via Pauli operations. After that, we suggest the Walsh-Hadamard transform and some approximation method for decoding the convolution equation to estimate the tailored noise. We prove that constant sampling and polynomial time complexities are sufficient to guarantee bounded noise estimation error with respect to the $l_2$-norm, which usually requires exponential complexity with existing noise estimation methods. The polynomial complexities are maintained even for the more stringent $l_1$ approximation under the sparse noise assumption. Conclusively, we propose novel methods for characterizing the noise properties of an entangled state at a lower cost than that of state generation. Moreover, compared with state verification methods, we can attain richer information on noise rates and enable noise mitigation, thereby providing guarantees for the preparation of graph states.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Feature Extraction
abstract: This paper presents an innovative approach to quantum data analysis, focusing on the automated extraction of key features through the application of a quantum algorithm. The core aim is to improve the efficiency of data processing by leveraging the inherent properties of quantum systems to identify subtle patterns and correlations within data. We introduce a novel system that dynamically adapts to the data's characteristics, ensuring optimal feature extraction for a wide range of quantum datasets. The system employs a quantum algorithm specifically designed for pattern recognition, resulting in a significantly enhanced analysis process. This research addresses a critical challenge in quantum data science – the need for efficient and automated feature discovery – offering a potential paradigm shift in data processing methodologies.

title: Quantum State Adaptive Computing: Towards Adaptive and Secure Quantum Computation
abstract: Quantum state adaptive computing represents a paradigm shift in quantum information processing, moving beyond traditional algorithms to leverage the inherent adaptability of quantum states. This paper explores the potential of this approach to design quantum algorithms and computation models that exhibit self-adaptation, crucial for addressing security vulnerabilities and enabling a wider range of applications. We introduce the core claim that utilizing quantum state adaptability allows for the creation of quantum computation systems with enhanced resilience and security. Our mechanism centers on strategically employing quantum information security algorithms to safeguard quantum information throughout its lifecycle. The paper details a novel design for adaptive quantum algorithms and computational models, emphasizing the crucial role of quantum state adaptability in achieving robust and secure quantum systems. The research explores the benefits and challenges of this approach, highlighting its potential impact on the future of quantum computing.

title: Formal Verification Program Generation (FVPG)
abstract: This paper explores the emerging field of Formal Verification Program Generation (FVPG), a novel approach to software development that leverages the power of formal verification techniques to automatically generate programs satisfying specified security and performance constraints. The core concept involves integrating formal verification methods with program generation methodologies. A verification engine is employed to generate program code segments that adhere to the established constraints, which are subsequently assembled into complete, functional programs. This approach offers a potential solution to the increasing complexity and criticality of software systems, where guaranteeing correctness and reliability is paramount. We outline the fundamental principles, potential challenges, and future directions of this rapidly developing area. The key contribution lies in the automated bridge between rigorous verification and practical program synthesis, opening avenues for developing demonstrably correct and efficient software.

title: Quantum Topology for Probabilistic Machine Learning
abstract: Quantum topology, a field of physics and mathematics, describes geometric structures that exhibit unusual properties of entanglement and non-locality. This paper explores the application of quantum topology to probabilistic machine learning, focusing on the design of a model leveraging quantum spin states and rotations to learn data distributions and predict outcomes. We propose a novel approach that utilizes the inherent quantum properties of spacetime to create a probabilistic model capable of enhanced prediction and classification. The core mechanism involves mapping data into a quantum state, allowing the model to exploit entanglement and superposition to achieve superior performance. This research addresses the limitations of traditional machine learning algorithms by introducing a fundamentally different approach based on quantum principles. The benefits include improved robustness, adaptability, and the potential for uncovering hidden patterns within complex data.

title: The Adaptive Quantum Algorithm Probability Model
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive quantum algorithm probability model, designed to enhance the optimization and stability of quantum algorithms. Traditional quantum algorithms often rely on static parameters, while this research focuses on probabilistic models, enabling efficient parameter tuning and improved performance. We present a framework for constructing probabilistic models that translate quantum algorithm execution into distribution functions, leveraging the inherent properties of probability to guide optimization. The core mechanism centers around exploiting quantum algorithms' unique characteristics to create a probabilistic representation of the computation, enabling targeted parameter adjustments to improve algorithm performance. The novel contribution lies in the integration of this probabilistic model into a robust optimization framework, addressing a critical challenge in the design and application of quantum algorithms.

title: Probabilistic Grammatical Inference with Bayesian Hidden Markov Models
abstract: This paper presents a novel Bayesian approach to probabilistic grammatical inference, specifically designed for learning context-free grammars (CFGs) from noisy and incomplete data. The core idea revolves around integrating Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) to model the underlying linguistic structures, effectively handling the inherent uncertainties present in real-world language data. We utilize variational inference to approximate the posterior distribution of the CFG parameters, with the HMMs providing a robust framework for representing and propagating uncertainty in transition probabilities. The resulting model offers a significant improvement over traditional CFG learning methods, particularly in scenarios where data is sparse, ambiguous, or contains significant noise. This approach provides a more robust and adaptable solution for language modeling tasks, addressing limitations of existing techniques by explicitly acknowledging and modeling uncertainty within the grammatical structure itself. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and a conceptual outline of its implementation, paving the way for future research and practical applications. ---

title: 基于量子退相干的通信协议优化
abstract: This paper investigates the optimization of quantum communication protocols leveraging the phenomenon of quantum decoherence. Traditional quantum communication protocols frequently rely on fixed parameter settings, often neglecting the dynamic influence of decoherence on channel performance. We propose a framework for dynamically adjusting protocol parameters based on real-time decoherence measurements. This framework aims to maximize communication efficiency and security by exploiting the controllable nature of decoherence. Specifically, we explore the relationship between interaction strength, decoherence time, and key protocol parameters such as pulse duration and detuning. The core claim is that by controlling these factors, optimal performance can be achieved. The proposed method offers a potential pathway to enhancing quantum communication robustness and scalability. Mathematical formulations are presented to quantify the impact of these parameters and guide the optimization process.

title: Looking Things Up Before Speaking: A Comparative Analysis Review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of RAG and retrieval as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Quantum Entanglement Computation via Dynamic Topology Simplification
abstract: Quantum entanglement remains a cornerstone of quantum computing, offering unparalleled computational capabilities. However, harnessing its full potential is hampered by the inherent computational complexity arising from entangled states. This paper presents a novel quantum entanglement computation framework, leveraging dynamic topology simplification (DTS) to dramatically reduce this complexity and enhance the efficiency of information storage and utilization. We propose a method to transform the complex entanglement landscape into a simplified, topologically driven structure, utilizing this structure to guide the computation and optimize information handling. The core claim is that this approach significantly lowers entanglement calculation complexity and improves the utilization of entangled information. This work explores the potential of DTS to unlock new computational avenues and address key limitations in quantum entanglement applications.

title: Quantum Neural Networks: Adaptive Activation for Enhanced Efficiency
abstract: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) represent a paradigm shift in machine learning, leveraging the unique properties of quantum systems to potentially surpass classical neural networks. However, the inherent complexity of quantum systems presents significant challenges in designing efficient and adaptable architectures. This paper explores the integration of adaptive activation functions into QNNs to address this challenge. We propose a novel mechanism for dynamically adjusting activation function parameters, fostering increased efficiency and improved model performance. The core of our work lies in a system that employs a feedback loop, iteratively refining the activation function based on the network's internal state and the task at hand. This adaptive process significantly reduces computational costs compared to static activation functions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and preliminary experiments, showcasing enhanced performance in a targeted task. The resulting QNN exhibits superior results in terms of accuracy and speed, highlighting the potential of this novel activation mechanism.

title: Neural Symbolic Causal Reasoning Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework, Neural Symbolic Causal Reasoning Networks (NSCRN), that integrates the strengths of neural networks and symbolic causal reasoning engines to achieve robust and interpretable modeling and prediction of complex system dynamics. The core idea is to build a hierarchical neural network where lower layers extract sensory data and patterns, while higher layers perform symbolic causal inference. This leverages graph structures to represent causal relationships and facilitates backward causal inference, guiding the activity of the neural network. Unlike existing methods that rely solely on neural or symbolic approaches, NSCRN combines these paradigms to offer enhanced reasoning capabilities, particularly in handling uncertainty and noise inherent in real-world systems. The framework addresses limitations of purely neural models in representing causality and purely symbolic models in dealing with noisy data. The primary contribution lies in the architecture and the integration of causal inference within a deep learning framework, leading to improved predictive accuracy and explainability. The system is designed to learn causal relationships directly from data while leveraging symbolic reasoning for precise and reliable inference. We demonstrate the potential of NSCRN through a conceptual framework, outlining the key components and their interactions.

title: ##基于多模态感知融合的自适应知识图谱构建
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to constructing and maintaining knowledge graphs (KGs) through multimodal perception fusion and adaptive reasoning. The core idea is to leverage diverse data modalities – including visual, auditory, and textual information – to autonomously build and dynamically update KGs. The system employs a multimodal perception module to transform these raw data into unified vector representations. An attention mechanism is then utilized to weigh the contributions of each modality based on its relevance and reliability. The fused information is subsequently integrated with a knowledge graph reasoning engine, facilitating tasks such as entity recognition, relation extraction, knowledge inference, and knowledge update. This approach overcomes the limitations of traditional KG construction methods, which heavily rely on manual annotation, resulting in increased coverage, accuracy, and adaptability of the knowledge graph. The system demonstrates the potential for real-time KG construction and dynamic updates in scenarios requiring continuous knowledge acquisition and refinement. ---

title: Efficient Abstractive Text Summarization with Large Language Models: A Focused Survey
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly improved the quality of abstractive text summarization. However, the high computational cost and memory requirements of these models limit their practical adoption, particularly in resource-constrained environments. This focused survey reviews recent progress in efficient LLM-based abstractive text summarization, emphasizing methods designed to operate under realistic hardware constraints. The survey first provides a concise background on abstractive and extreme summarization, highlighting challenges introduced by long contexts and aggressive compression. A structured taxonomy is then proposed to categorize existing approaches according to model architecture, training strategy, adaptation technique, and hardware awareness. Building on this taxonomy, the paper analyzes key efficiency-oriented techniques, including parameter-efficient fine-tuning, low-bit quantization, precision optimization, and inference-time acceleration. Furthermore, commonly used evaluation protocols are reviewed, emphasizing the limitations of traditional automated metrics and the growing need for faithfulness- and cost-aware evaluation. A comparative discussion summarizes trade-offs between summarization quality and computational efficiency, offering practical guidelines for model selection and deployment. Finally, open challenges and future research directions are outlined, including faithful extreme summarization, long-context processing, multimodal summarization, and standardized efficiency-aware benchmarks. Overall, this survey provides researchers and practitioners with a clear, structured overview of practical considerations for efficient LLM-based text summarization.

Building on this taxonomy, the paper analyzes key efficiency-oriented techniques, including parameter-efficient fine-tuning, low-bit quantization, precision optimization, and inference-time acceleration. Furthermore, commonly used evaluation protocols are reviewed, emphasizing the limitations of traditional automated metrics and the growing need for faithfulness- and cost-aware evaluation. A comparative discussion summarizes trade-offs between summarization quality and computational efficiency, offering practical guidelines for model selection and deployment. Finally, open challenges and future research directions are outlined, including faithful extreme summarization, long-context processing, multimodal summarization, and standardized efficiency-aware benchmarks. Overall, this survey provides researchers and practitioners with a clear, structured overview of practical considerations for efficient LLM-based text summarization.

title: Readout failures in superconducting qubits due to two-level system defects in tunnel junctions
abstract: Material defects give rise to parasitic two-level systems (TLS) that present a major source of decoherence in superconducting qubits. Here, we study a strongly coupled TLS that resides in the tunnel barrier of transmon qubit. We use multiphoton spectroscopy and TLS strain tuning to explore the rich spectrum of the interacting three-partite system consisting of TLS, qubit, and its readout resonator. This reveals a strong effective resonant coupling between the TLS and the qubit's readout resonator, which dresses the resonator states and results in a resonance frequency shift that spoils the readout signal. Our finding presents yet another way how material defects can interfere with qubit operation and hinder the realization of solid-state quantum processors.

title: Multimodal collaborative modeling of teacher verbal and non-verbal classroom behaviors for teaching effectiveness prediction
abstract: Abstract Teacher classroom behavior sits at the centre of any serious attempt to understand and improve instructional quality, yet the verbal and the non-verbal channel are still typically examined apart, which leaves their pedagogically meaningful interdependence unmodelled. This paper proposes a multimodal deep learning framework that models the two channels collaboratively and predicts teaching effectiveness from their joint representation. Four modules compose the framework: temporal synchronization of the audio and video streams, parallel unimodal encoding through BERT-based language representation and SlowFast spatiotemporal networks, bidirectional cross-modal attention fusion regulated by a gated modality weighting mechanism, and a dual-head prediction network optimized jointly for effectiveness classification and continuous score regression. On a corpus of 186 classroom sessions recorded in 12 schools, the framework attains 82.3% classification accuracy, 80.1% macro-F1, an RMSE of 6.58 and a Pearson correlation of 0.879, ahead of ten comparison systems spanning unimodal, traditional machine learning and state-of-the-art multimodal fusion approaches. Ablation identifies bidirectional cross-modal attention as the component that matters most, and an attention analysis conducted across all test sessions indicates that verbal-gestural temporal synchrony accompanies higher observer-rated teaching effectiveness. The framework thus offers a scalable, automated route from multimodal teacher behavior to instructional outcomes, with potential applications in teacher professional development and intelligent classroom observation systems.

title: Differentiable Electricity-Market Clearing for Gradient-Based Planning
abstract: Planning a large data center is difficult because a facility big enough to matter changes the electricity prices it will pay. Those prices are set by market clearing, a constrained optimization problem solved anew in every operating condition. However, simulating the market tells a planner how a candidate plan performs but not how to improve it. Here we treat market clearing as a differentiable optimization layer: each forward pass solves the market, and reverse-mode automatic differentiation propagates the planning cost back through the cleared prices to the plan. After validating these gradients against finite differences, we apply them to a concrete problem: allocating 50 MW of data-center load across six candidate buses in two synthetic networks, under a fixed cost per active site, evaluated over 36 operating states. Judged against exhaustive enumeration of all site combinations, gradient optimization recovers the continuous allocations almost exactly, with worst-case objective gaps of 2.3\% and 8.5\% of the cost difference between the best and worst single site. Its one systematic error is instructive: near the costs at which a site should close, the smooth relaxation of the discrete site count shrinks the site rather than closing it, so discrete transitions arrive late. Differentiable market clearing thus turns market-aware planning into a problem gradients can search.

title: Counterfactual Behavior Cloning: Offline Imitation Learning from Imperfect Human Demonstrations
abstract: Learning from humans is challenging because people are imperfect teachers. When everyday humans show the robot a new task they want it to perform, humans inevitably make errors (e.g., inputting noisy actions) and provide suboptimal examples (e.g., overshooting the goal). Existing methods often learn by matching some or all of the human's behavior — but this approach is fundamentally limited because the demonstrations themselves are imperfect. In this work we advance offline imitation learning by enabling robots to extrapolate across nearby actions, instead of only considering what the human actually showed. We achieve this by hypothesizing that all of the human's demonstrations are trying to convey an underlying policy, while the noise and sub-optimality within their behaviors obfuscates the data and introduces unintentional complexity. To recover the underlying policy and learn what the human teacher meant, we introduce Counter-BC , a generalized version of behavior cloning. Counter-BC expands the given dataset to include actions close to behaviors the human demonstrated (i.e., counterfactual actions that the human teacher could have intended, but did not actually show). During training Counter-BC autonomously modifies the human's demonstrations within this expanded region to reach a simplified policy that explains the underlying trends in the human's dataset. Theoretically, we prove that Counter-BC can extract a simple and similar-to-demonstration policy from imperfect data, multiple users, and teachers of varying skill levels. Empirically, we compare Counter-BC to state-of-the-art alternatives in simulated and real-world settings with noisy demonstrations, standardized datasets, and real human teachers. Overall, we find that trying to extrapolate what the human teacher meant by considering nearby actions — as opposed to rigorously following what actions the human actually demonstrated — can lead to more proficient learning from humans. See videos of our work here: https://youtu.be/XaeOZWhTt68

title: Prompt Engineering: Theory, Techniques and Practice
abstract: This textbook aims to offer an in-depth, accessible, and hands-on exploration of prompt engineering the art of creating inputs that enable large language models to deliver more accurate, reliable, and suitable responses. It meets the needs of undergraduate and postgraduate students in computer science, artificial intelligence and the data sciences as well as practicing engineers, data scientists and AI product managers who want to learn prompt engineering from a research-based perspective.Prompt engineering has been a rapidly flowering field of study. Interacting with AI systems effectively used to need a dedicated data scientist with experience in machine learning, model architecture and train infrastructure and just a few years ago! Natural language is the main gateway to the most powerful AI systems ever created and the main factor in how good that gateway is, is the quality of natural language that is used as input. This has made AI more accessible and, at the same time, a brand new specialized branch: the art and science of developing the AI optimized prompts.The textbook consists of five units which progress from basic concepts to advanced techniques and onto the forefront of research. Unit I lays the theoretical and empirical groundwork, covering the architecture of large language models (LLM), natural language processing (NLP) and generative AI basics, using prompts to control the outputs of LLMs, the main categories of prompting—zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot, and model deep-dives into the world's most popular models such as ChatGPT, GPT-4 and GPT-4.5, Claude, Gemini, and LLaMA. Unit II covers best practices in iterative prompt refinement, contextual prompting with examples and constraints, and chain-of-thought prompting and instruction-based prompting, all key steps in prompt design. Unit III introduces more complex prompting approaches such as multi-turn, self-consistency & verification prompts, prompt decomposition, prompt reusability, and other advanced methods like Tree of Thoughts, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, few shot with demonstrations. Unit IV will explore the tools, frameworks and applications that make up the current state of deployed prompt engineering, including a detailed look at Langchain, LlamaIndex and Haystack along with prompt evaluation metrics and applications like education, business automation, coding assistance, content generation and more. In Unit V, students will discover the burgeoning research landscape of autonomous agents and prompt chaining, fine-tuning versus prompt engineering, prompt engineering using external knowledge bases, ethical concerns and responsible AI prompting, exciting future research and development opportunities in multimodal prompting and human-AI creative collaboration, and the standardization of prompt engineering process.Extensive unit material is provided after each unit with a comprehensive review, unit summary tying the key concepts together, practical hands-on activities, and deep dive to explore the core content in greater detail for more advanced students. There are five appendices containing practical supporting content, including worked examples across real applications, prompt quality checklist & reusable prompts, API-specific prompting guidance, and ethical guidance for professional practice and specialized domain guidance – healthcare, legal, financial, creative.Original exposition in preference to borrowed formulations are used throughout this book. All material is designed to be done independently - no supplementary tools are needed. Conceptual explanations are followed by concrete examples, theoretical principles are illustrated with concrete examples, and worked examples are provided that trace the complete design process – from requirements analysis through iterative process of refining the design to deployment evaluation. The outcome is a thorough and complete guide to prompting as it is done at the cutting edge of the discipline.We hope that this textbook will not only lead to current practice in prompt engineering, but also provide a conceptual basis which will not end up being outdated as the field progresses. The actual models, tools and benchmark results will vary based on any new developments that come to light. The ethical principles, systematic experimentations, rigorous analysis, and clear communication upon which good prompt engineering is built will stand the test of time. How to use this textbookThis textbook is not meant to be read separately, but rather in order, so that one unit can supplement the content of the previous units. More technically oriented students may have background knowledge in neural networks and natural language processing and choose to skip over this material and start the prompting content in Chapter 3. Those who want to get to work with tools but aren't interested in the theory can start with Unit II, and go back to Unit I as necessary for theory.The books are structured in the same manner as the chapters. Core Content sections clearly explain and analyze the main concepts of content together with examples. These sections give "Base Information" necessary for better practice. This basic work is extended through review questions after each unit, which assess comprehension and application of the material; through unit summaries that relate key concepts; and through hands-on activities, that master skills and knowledge, and through deep-dives on section that explore selected topics in greater detail and at a more technical level.Exam Review / Practice Questions: To prepare for exams. Questions are structured from direct recall of definitions and concepts to comparative analysis of concepts, designing something, and critical assessment of design tradeoffs. Examinations candidates are asked to attempt all questions; professionals looking for knowledge refresh could choose questions most pertinent to their needs.Real-world exercises will be most useful with access to an LLM system. There are free or cheep tiers available for completion of exercises using the APIs from the cloud (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.) For those preferring an alternative model deployment platform, and those who prefer not to utilize the cloud, local model deployment via tools like Ollama is an option. Exercise describe the task but leave the final choice of which model to use to the practitioner: the same principles apply to the different models, although the results of the exercises are for each specific model.Appendices present information that are reference but not sequential. The prompt quality checklist in Appendix B is especially handy as a resource to reference as prompts are being developed. API-specific information should be used, at least initially, when using a new model provider, see Appendix C for guidance. For anyone using LLM applications in impact areas, Appendix D contains ethical guidelines that should be read carefully.One of the greatest benefits of the worked examples included in Appendix A is the opportunity they provide to gain insight into how abstract concepts are applied to real design decisions. Every example follows the entire process of application development, from requirements to the iterative process of refinement to evaluation and deployment. By reading through these examples and trying to understand not only the actual decision that was made, but why will help develop judgment to deal with new situations where there is no specific rule or template that can be applied.

title: DSPkit-app: a local web application for digital signal processing of time series data
abstract: DSPkit-app is a desktop application for digital signal processing of time series data, built on the DSPkit library. A file is opened without configuration: the delimiter, header row, orientation, time column and sample rate are detected on load and shown so they can be overridden, and the signals are plotted immediately. Analyses cover spectral estimation, cross-signal relationships, filtering with cutoffs picked off the spectrum, a linked time-frequency explorer over five transforms, decomposition, multi-channel coherence including conditioned forms, Frequency Domain Decomposition with mode shape export, and statistical analysis including normality assessment. It requires only Python 3.10 or newer; the interface ships pre-built and the analysis library is bundled, so no other tooling is needed to run it.

title: Benchmarking Personally Identifiable Information (PII) Anonymization Strategies for Brazilian Portuguese: From Regex to Hybrid LLM Approaches
authors: Joao Pedro Hallack Sansao and Thiago França Nascimento, Universidade Federal de Sao Joao del-Rei, Brazil
abstract: The Brazilian General Data Protection Law (LGPD) requires the anonymization of personally identifiable information (PII) before data sharing. We evaluate six anonymization strategies (regex, NER, zero-shot LLM, few-shot LLM, structured extraction, and a hybrid cascade) on 82 Brazilian Portuguese documents with 1,558 PII spans across 12 LLM variants. A hybrid cascade combining regex, NER, and conditional LLM invocation achieves 0.0% residual PII on the test set, matching text-to-text approaches while preserving span-level annotations. Model scale does not monotonically affect residual PII: Gemma 3-4B and Gemma 3-12B produce 2.28 and 1.56 residual respectively in zero-shot, while GPT-4o produces 3.71. The 38 strategy–model combinations provide a privacy–utility–cost analysis for Portuguese PII anonymization.

title: Quantum Entanglement Self-Organizing Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum algorithm, the Quantum Entanglement Self-Organizing Algorithm (QESA), designed to dynamically adjust system parameters within a complex system to optimize performance and stability. Leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement, QESA establishes a self-organizing mechanism that continuously refines parameter values based on real-time feedback, achieving a level of adaptability unattainable through conventional methods. The core mechanism centers on creating and manipulating entangled states to achieve this dynamic adjustment. This paper details the algorithm's architecture, the quantum operations involved, and the theoretical implications of its self-optimization capabilities. We present preliminary results demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness in a simplified system, highlighting its potential for broader applicability across diverse complex systems.

title: Rewards, Regrets, and Rubber Arms: A State of the Art Review of Reinforcement Learning in Games and Robotics
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Reinforcement Learning in Games and Robotics in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of reinforcement learning and robotics as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: 基于自适应的机器学习的概率模型优化
abstract: This paper presents a novel probabilistic model optimization technique centered around adaptive machine learning. Traditional machine learning methods often rely on static model parameters, limiting their ability to effectively handle data scarcity. We introduce a method that dynamically adjusts probability model parameters based on the data, leveraging the inherent adaptability of machine learning algorithms. This approach enhances model prediction accuracy and robustness, particularly when data is limited. The core mechanism involves an iterative adjustment process guided by a learning algorithm, ensuring the model adapts to the data distribution. We provide a theoretical framework and demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of simulations and experiments. The goal is to improve model performance in scenarios where data is sparse, offering a more robust and efficient solution compared to traditional approaches.

title: Non-Linear Integral-Based Gradient Boosting
abstract: This paper presents a novel gradient boosting algorithm, termed Non-Linear Integral-Based Gradient Boosting (NLIBG), designed to address the limitations of traditional gradient boosting methods. The core innovation lies in the implementation of an adaptive integration parameter strategy that dynamically adjusts the integration function during training, promoting better model generalization and reducing overfitting. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NLIBG through extensive experimental validation on a diverse range of machine learning and numerical datasets. The algorithm's automatic parameter adjustment mechanism significantly enhances the model's predictive performance compared to existing approaches. This work offers a promising pathway for enhancing the robustness and accuracy of gradient boosting algorithms.

title: Title: Adaptive Constraint Geometry
abstract: Abstract: Adaptive Constraint Geometry addresses the challenge of designing and optimizing constraint geometries for complex physical systems through the integration of evolutionary algorithms and reinforcement learning. Traditional methods often rely on manual definition, leading to brittle and suboptimal designs. This paper proposes a novel computational approach that automatically generates and refines constraint configurations using genetic algorithms, guided by a feedback metric that prioritizes both physical stability and efficiency. We present a framework for iterative refinement based on this feedback, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating designs suitable for modeling a range of physical systems. The core mechanism involves evolving constraint configurations through a genetic algorithm, incorporating a feedback metric that dynamically adjusts the design based on physical properties and performance criteria. The resulting designs exhibit enhanced stability and efficiency compared to conventional approaches, offering a significant advancement in automated constraint design.

title: Title: Bayesian Fractal Resonance
abstract: This paper introduces Bayesian Fractal Resonance, a novel probabilistic model designed to predict complex patterns across multiple scales within fractal geometries. The core mechanism leverages a Bayesian network that dynamically updates probability based on observed fractal structure, incorporating a 'resonance factor' to prioritize stable and complex arrangements. The goal is to move beyond static pattern recognition towards a model capable of simulating and predicting the evolution of complex fractal systems. This approach offers enhanced predictive power and allows for the simultaneous analysis of multiple scales. The paper details the model's architecture, explores the role of the resonance factor, and provides a conceptual framework for its application in various fields, including materials science, image processing, and pattern generation.

title: Neural Symbolic Systems for Robotic Planning and Control
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to robotic planning and control utilizing a synergistic combination of neural networks and symbolic reasoning. Current robotic systems often struggle with the complexities of real-world environments, exhibiting brittleness and a lack of adaptability. We argue that a hybrid system, leveraging the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks and the logical inference capabilities of symbolic systems, offers a more robust and effective solution. The core of our system consists of two key components: a high-level planning network that learns strategic plans and a symbolic reasoning engine that translates these plans into actionable commands for the robot. This architecture allows for both rapid adaptation to novel situations and the incorporation of explicit knowledge, leading to improved performance and reliability in robotic tasks. The system is designed to overcome the limitations of purely neural or purely symbolic approaches, creating a more intelligent and flexible robotic agent. This paper outlines the architecture, key components, and theoretical foundations of this Neural Symbolic System, and discusses potential applications and future research directions.

title: Quantum Homomorphic Computation Geometric Optimization
abstract: Quantum Homomorphic Computation (QHC) offers a fundamentally new approach to computation, leveraging the power of quantum mechanics to perform computations on encrypted data without decryption. This paper explores the application of geometric optimization to QHC, proposing a novel framework for enhancing the efficiency of hidden computation. We argue that traditional optimization methods often fall short in the complex, multi-dimensional space inherent to QHC, and that geometric optimization provides a crucial step towards achieving significant performance improvements. Our work demonstrates the potential of this approach through a rigorous analysis and preliminary results, highlighting its implications for future advancements in secure and efficient computation.

title: Algorithm Complexity and Nonlinear Functions
abstract: This paper explores the interplay between algorithm complexity and nonlinear functions, proposing a novel concept of "Nonlinear Function Complexity" (NFC) to identify and mitigate potential inefficiencies within existing algorithms. Traditional complexity measures primarily focus on execution time, while nonlinear functions offer a deeper insight into the algorithmic process. We define NFC as a metric derived from analyzing algorithm complexity, highlighting non-linear dependencies within the code. This approach utilizes this metric to pinpoint areas for optimization, ultimately leading to more efficient algorithms. The goal is to provide a robust framework for analyzing and improving the performance of complex systems. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of algorithm design and optimization, particularly in scenarios involving nonlinear functions.

title: Self-Organizing Quantum Neural Networks for Optimal Resource Allocation
abstract: This paper investigates the application of self-organizing quantum neural networks (SQNNs) to the problem of optimal resource allocation, a core challenge across diverse domains including finance, logistics, and telecommunications. Traditional classical neural networks frequently struggle to achieve optimal solutions when faced with complex constraints and dynamic environments. The central hypothesis of this work is that leveraging quantum computation through SQNNs, specifically utilizing qubit representations of resource states and exploiting entanglement, can significantly enhance the exploration of the solution space and lead to near-optimal resource allocation decisions. We propose a novel SQNN architecture designed to address this challenge. The architecture incorporates layers of quantum neurons that dynamically adjust their connectivity based on the input data, mimicking the self-organizing properties observed in biological neural networks. We present a theoretical framework outlining the key components of the SQNN and detail the mathematical formulation of the resource allocation problem being addressed. The core of the model is expressed as follows: Let *N* be the number of resources to be allocated. Let *K* be the number of potential allocation options for each resource. Let *xi* represent the allocation decision for resource *i*, where *xi* ∈ {1, 2, ..., *K*}. The objective is to minimize the cost function *C(x)*, which is defined as: *C(x) = ∑i=1N *Ci(xi)* where *Ci(xi)* represents the cost associated with resource *i* given the allocation *xi*. This cost function is subject to constraints *G(x) ≤ 0*, where *G* is a vector of constraints representing factors like capacity limits, demand requirements, and regulatory restrictions. The SQNN learns to approximate the optimal solution *x* that minimizes *C(x)* subject to the constraints *G(x) ≤ 0*. The network's self-organizing capability is achieved through a modified backpropagation algorithm adapted for quantum systems, incorporating quantum measurement and entangling operations to refine the network's internal state and improve its ability to represent and optimize the resource allocation problem. The efficacy of the SQNN is evaluated through simulations, demonstrating its potential to outperform classical neural networks in complex resource allocation scenarios.

title: A COMPARATIVE STUDY OF CNN-BILSTM AND TF-IDF–NAIVE BAYES FOR SENTIMENT CLASSIFICATION ON MOVIE REVIEWS: PERFORMANCE AND EFFICIENCY TRADE-OFFS
abstract: Sentiment analysis on movie reviews has become an important task for understanding public opinion, yet many high-performing deep learning models proposed in the literature rely on increasingly complex architectures such as multichannel embeddings, kernel-based projections, or attention-augmented transformers. This added complexity often comes without a clear report of computational cost, making it difficult to judge whether the performance gain justifies the resource trade-off. This study investigates whether a deliberately simplified Convolutional Neural Network combined with a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-BiLSTM) architecture can achieve competitive performance compared to a classical baseline, TF-IDF combined with Naive Bayes, while explicitly reporting training efficiency. Both models were trained and evaluated on the IMDB Dataset of 50,000 movie reviews, split into 80% training, 10% validation, and 10% testing sets. Experimental results show that the proposed CNN-BiLSTM achieved an accuracy of 86.58%, precision of 90.38%, recall of 81.88%, F1-score of 85.92%, and AUC of 0.946, while the TF-IDF-Naive Bayes baseline achieved an accuracy of 85.98%, precision of 86.58%, recall of 85.16%, F1-score of 85.86%, and AUC of 0.932. The proposed method required approximately 203 seconds of training time, compared to 0.07 seconds for the baseline. These findings indicate that the performance improvement offered by the deep learning approach is modest relative to its substantially higher computational cost, providing practical guidance for method selection in resource-constrained settings.

title: Linguistic Foundations for Constructing Speech Synthesis in the Kazakh Language
abstract: The article is devoted to the problem of correctly recognizing and pronouncing, in accordance with orthoepic norms, shortened words and abbreviations, numerical symbols, mathematical operations, formulas, and conventional signs within the Kazakh-language text-to-speech system. The main objective of the study is to identify the linguistic features of fully expanding shortened words and abbreviations in texts processed by the speech synthesis system, as well as of representing mathematical expressions in written form, and on this basis to develop a linguistic resource that ensures natural, consistent, and realistic synthesized speech in Kazakh. The article clarifies the distinction between shortened words and abbreviations and proposes several approaches to incorporating them into a speech synthesis program. In particular, it describes methods such as compiling comprehensive lists of shortened forms from domain-specific texts, presenting shortened and full variants in parallel, and preserving internationally established abbreviations in their original forms. The article also provides a dedicated phonetic transcription of shortened words and demonstrates their pronunciation in compliance with orthoepic norms. The article presents model examples of attaching suffixes to shortened words, numerical symbols, and conventional signs in accordance with the vowel harmony rules of the Kazakh language. It is demonstrated that presenting both written and spoken variants of numerical symbols, arithmetic operations, fractions, and complex numbers increases the intelligibility of synthesized text. Furthermore, the parallel use of symbolic representations and established names of chemical elements and formulas is shown to enhance the naturalness of speech synthesis.

title: Reconfigurable measurement scheme compatible with MDI-QKD and BB84 protocols using single-laser sideband generation
abstract: A quantum network can be operated efficiently by switching between measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) and BB84 according to the trust level of an intermediate node, since MDI-QKD is immune to all detector side-channel attacks while generally yielding a lower secret-key rate. Here, we present a proof-of-principle demonstration of a reconfigurable measurement scheme compatible with both protocols using a single laser. Two mutually independent weak coherent states (WCSs) are generated from a shared continuous-wave laser via electro-optic phase modulation and subsequent first-order sideband filtering. Channel indistinguishability is verified using two complementary Hong–Ou–Mandel (HOM) measurements: time-resolved coincidence measurements and polarization mismatch scans, both yielding HOM visibilities close to the theoretical limit of 0.5 for WCSs. The measurement module performs a partial Bell-state measurement for MDI-QKD, while rotating a single half-wave plate to reconfigures the same module into a dual-basis polarization analyzer for BB84. The quantum bit error rates measured in both configurations agree well with theoretical expectations, verifying the operational feasibility of the reconfigurable receiver at the physical layer. By eliminating the need for active frequency locking while retaining independent sideband tunability, this approach provides a practical foundation for flexible and cost-effective quantum networks.

title: Toollery: Scaling LLM Agents to Thousands of Skills and Tools
abstract: As LLM agents are exposed to hundreds to tens of thousands of skills, tools, and API functions, full-library prompting becomes costly, slow, and less reliable: each added candidate increases prompt tokens and latency, while longer candidate lists introduce more distractors for LLM selection. We present \textbf{Toollery}, a training-free candidate-compression framework for scalable LLM skill/tool selection. Following established document-side query expansion, Toollery generates user-intent queries from each skill/tool specification and builds a retrieval index that maps real user requests to compact candidate sets before final LLM decision-making. By treating high-level skills and atomic tools as selectable capabilities, Toollery can be applied to both skill libraries and tool registries. We evaluate Toollery on the roughly 79K-capability SkillRouter benchmark, BFCL-V4 with over 440 atomic tools, and 3,396 proprietary smart-cockpit requests over 220 tools. Across these settings, Toollery keeps online selection bounded to a compact top-$k$ candidate set and improves recall over ordinary specification retrieval. At a fixed top-10 budget, Toollery improves end-to-end selection on the cockpit dataset, and maintains comparable AST Accuracy on BFCL-V4. These results support Toollery as a practical candidate-compression framework for large and evolving agent capability libraries, while showing that quality and cost gains depend on workload coverage and provider caching.

title: LeanStream: A Speculate-and-Refine Streaming Framework for Efficient on-Device LLM Inference
abstract: On-device LLM inference is attractive for privacy and responsiveness, but remains challenging on mobile and embedded devices because model weights far exceed available DRAM. Prior systems exploit activation sparsity and offload weights to SSD or flash storage, but face a fundamental systems trade-off: accurate sparse execution decisions require the latest context, whereas efficient computation-I/O overlap requires early prediction. As a result, existing designs either serialize execution or incur redundant weight fetches, extra computation, and large cache overheads. We present LeanStream, a streaming speculate-and-refine framework for efficient on-device LLM inference. LeanStream progressively refines computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results, enabling fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O. We implement LeanStream on both mobile and embedded platforms. Compared with prior on-device LLM inference systems, LeanStream reduces memory usage by 4.8$\times$ to 7.5$\times$ at the best throughput achieved by prior work, while further improving token generation throughput by 1.6$\times$ to 2.1$\times$.

title: Learning to Attract and Repel: Dual Quality Margin Learning for Face Recognition (DQM-Face)
abstract: Face recognition in unconstrained environments remains highly challenging due to diverse and extreme variations encountered in real-world scenarios. To mitigate these effects, existing margin-based approaches model sample quality through feature magnitude. However, magnitude-based modeling alone is susceptible to identity-agnostic noise, which can degrade the reliability and discriminative power of learned representations. In this paper, we propose Dual Quality Margin Learning for Face Recognition (DQM-Face), a novel framework that enables refined attraction and repulsion dynamics during representation learning. Our approach unifies conventional magnitude-based quality estimation with a newly introduced semantic quality learning mechanism, realized via squeeze-and-excitation semantic attention. By jointly leveraging magnitude and semantic cues, we construct enhanced quality-aware margins that adaptively strengthen intra-class compactness through improved attraction during learning. To further enhance inter-class discrimination, we introduce a repulsion margin formulation that explicitly enlarges inter-class separation. The unified integration of semantic quality modeling with dual attraction-repulsion margin optimization results in a more structured and discriminative feature geometry. Extensive experiments on multiple challenging benchmarks demonstrate that DQM-Face consistently outperforms state-of-the-art face recognition methods. Moreover, we show that the quality learned for margin optimization is highly effective for face image quality assessment within the proposed framework, demonstrating that the learned quality signal is intrinsically aligned with the recognition objective. The code is publicly available: https://github.com/RAIB-group/DQM-Face
